lg.l: [The confidante’s] refusal [of the bard] at the door; [the bard] speaking at the door;
the confidante rebuking [the bard]; [the bard’s] vexation appearing;
the hero becoming vexed; the heroine becoming vexed;
[the heroine] saying, ‘He, the lover, does not desire me’;
the mother seeing [this] and speaking; and other [situations] that exist

because of enduring love – [these are] the separation to that place.This, as is made clear in the commentary, is a way to refer to the hero’s separation when he is visiting his extramarital lover, referred to in this translation as ‘the other woman’. It is not clear, however, exactly how to translate the phrase āyiṭai pirivu. The most common translations are ‘intermediate-distance separation’ or ‘separation to that place’. The second is preferred in part due to its ambiguity. For the sake of clarity, āyiṭai is a combination of the deictic prefix a- (‘that, there’) and the noun iṭai (‘place’). Both convey the idea that this separation is both short-term, at least compared to the long-distance version mentioned in the previous cūttiram, and short-distance, as the hero’s other woman is understood to live in the same town as the hero and heroine by theoreticians. The translation ‘that place’ allows for an elliptical reference to the fact that he is going somewhere he should not by stepping out of his marital home, and it also keeps open the possibility that it can be a separation to a place that is right there.

div.p: eṉpatu āy iṭaip pirivām āṟuṇarttutaṉutaliṟṟu.
The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which the separation to ‘that place’ occurs.
vāyiṉ maṟuttal mutal ākac cevili kūṟṟīṟākac collap paṭṭa vivaiyum piṟavum parattaiyiṟ pirivām eṉṟa vāṟu.
Beginning with ‘the refusal at the door’ and ending with ‘the foster-mother’s speech’, these that have been mentioned and others are the separation on account of the other woman.
piṟavum eṉṟataṉāṟ parattaiyar kūṟṟum pūppuṇarttutalum uḷ ḷiṭṭaṉa vellāṅ koḷka.
By piṟavum, understand that all of the speeches of the other woman and the making known of menstruation are included.

lg.l: Because he is a base man, the words from your mouth are lies.

Don’t stand there, bard. Leave now and do not grieve!The point of this negative imperative, pariyal, is seemingly to soften the effect of her rebuke on the bard – he ought not to feel so hurt; her anger is really directed at the hero.
If our quarter sees [him] under the sun,

the man from the village with vast paddy-fields will Is the implication here that the hero will feel the same shame that the heroine feels when spotted? Or does the ummai on nāṇavum carry a more emphatic sense, as translated? The placement on nāṇa rather than ūraṉ suggests the latter to me. obtain even shame.

div.p: eṉpatu pāṇaṉukku vāyiṉ maṟuttatu.
This is [the confidante] having refused the bard at the door.

lg.l: …This is only a partial translation, but it is possible as not much text is lost, and one can guess based on the length of the missing chunk and its position that it was probably a phrase qualifying the ‘goodness’. I will indeed now speak of [his] goodness,

please don’t slap [me]!Partially due to the missing first two cīr, it is unclear who is the object of alaiyātīmē – the hero or the bard. The meaning of the verb can also be taken differently. Rather than the immediate and rather violent ‘to slap’, chosen here on the strength of Caṅkam attestations of the negative imperatives of the same root (AN 158.7 and AN 190.6, for example), this can also mean ‘to harass’.

div.p: eṉpatu vāyiṉ maṟukkappaṭṭa pāṇaṉ kūṟiyatu.
This is the bard, who had been refused at the door, having spoken.

lg.l: … the foolish one with a brilliant forehead
does not understand what the man from the village did.
[it is] as though she had not experienced [it].
Alas, she scolded [him] because of her [angry] nature.

div.p: eṉpatu viṟali vāyiṉ maṟuttatu.
This is the dancing-girl having been refused at the door.

lg.l: … the intimacy of the man from the village with ponds in nice divisionsWe find a parallel for this kind of usage of the phrase am kaṇ as a qualification of a part of a village in NA 210.1, where it refers to the pleasing division of fields. Without the preceding line for context, I take this interpretation.

it is there one day a month, O friend!Two lines of the poem have been lost. This is necessarily a speculative translation, but it makes some sense in the context of the poetic situation suggested by the koḷu.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻikku vāyiṉ maṟuttatu.
This is [the heroine] having refused the confidante at the door.

lg.l: ‘Surely the watchmen will come here’, thinking [this],
as [her] red mouth quivered like the petals of the coral tree,

[the one with] excellent long streaked eyes – did she not redden?The normal connotation that reddening of the eyes has is sadness – eyes become red because of crying. cē-ttal, however, can also mean ‘to become angry’. Considering the other poems in this section, anger rather than sadness seems to be the dominant emotion experienced by the heroine. The poet may have been playing with this double connotation.

div.p: eṉpatu vāyiṉ maṟuttamai tōḻi talaimakaṟkuc colliyatu.
This is the confidante having spoken to the hero about [the heroine’s] refusal at the door.

lg.l: O heart, how greatly we suffer!

I did not even obtain the door forI am not sure how to understand mutal here, and I see two viable options. As taken in the translation, it means ‘basis, reason’, and the hero is complaining that even for the reason of the feast, he was unable to re-enter the marital home. Another interpretation is to understand it in the sense of ‘beginning’, in which case this could simply be referring to ‘the beginning of the feast’, when he was denied entry. the feast.
The [one of] hips with perfect jewels will not give up [her] anger.

div.p: eṉpatu vāyil peṟāta talaimakaṉ vāṭiyatu.
This is the hero, who had not obtained the door, having grieved.

lg.l: Having gone [to her], I know of [the one]

who today thinksThe confidante can also be the agent of niṉaii, in which case she would feel bad about what she said when refusing the hero (or the bard) entry to the house, and would now want to make it up to him by helping resolve the lovers’ quarrel. all the words spoken yesterday

a mistake, arisen in turn,This is not at all clear. The base meaning of ūḻi in the old corpus is an ‘era/aeon’, which makes no sense in this context. According to the TL, it can mean ‘fate’. This would work here – the heroine would understand that their argument was simply her lot in life, which would lessen the blame on the hero. In the attestation cited for this entry, I am not convinced that this is its meaning and I have not found another example where it means that. This translation takes the meaning found in PN 370, ‘a turn’, in this case of a new day or some other period of time. and counts me as a companion.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ āṟṟāmai kaṇṭūṭal uṇarttac cellun tōḻi colliyatu.
This is the confidante, who had gone to resolve [the lovers’] quarrel, having spoken [to the hero] after seeing the heroine unable to bear [the situation].

lg.l: The anger of [the one with]Without having a clear read on the poetic situation, which we do not, as nearly all the koḷu has been lost, it is impossible to be certain about the intention of the poet, and thus this poem can be interpreted in different ways. As translated, it is an address by the confidante to the hero, perhaps counselling him on the correct way to approach the heroine so as to defuse the febrile situation. One could, however, just as well imagine this as the hero’s address to the confidante, expressing some exasperation at the anger he faces from the heroine. To do so would require a change not in how the poem is construed, but simply in who is the speaker. The other reasonable option, as I see it, is to construe differently and to take this as the address of the confidante to the heroine. naṟu nutal in the final line then has to be understood as an unmarked vocative aṉmoḻittokai: ‘O [one with] the fragrant forehead, anger because… is it right? It is not!’ the fragrant forehead
because of [your] entrance with the ruddy-haired son upon [your] chest

with red marksOr ‘fine’ (cem) marks. I cannot really disambiguate between the two here, and it is not clear to me what the significance of these marks is. Perhaps they are signs of the affair with the parattai, in which case ‘red marks’ makes good sense. However, they might simply be marks of beauty, in which case ‘fine’ is possibly more appropriate. and that bears the five weapons [of Viṣṇu]This is a reference to the tāli – a specific amulet worn for protection where the pendant is decorated with the five weapons of Viṣṇu.
– Is it a good thing? It is not!

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi…

standOff.note: Cf. TP150n.25–26: pāṇar kūttar viṟaliya reṉṟivar | pēṇic colliya kuṟaiviṉai yetiru
Cf. TP500n.3–4: pulaviyu mūṭalu muṇarvum | pirivoṭu puṇarntatu kaṟpeṉap paṭumē ||
Cf. TP156n: uṇarppuvarai yiṟappiṉuñ ceykuṟi piḻaippiṉum | pulattalu mūṭaluṅ kiḻavōṟ kuriya ||
Cf. IA47: kiḻavōṉ muṉṉark kiḻatti kaṟpukaḻtal | pulavik kālattum puraiva taṉṟē ||
Cf. IA48: nāṭu mūru milluñ cuṭṭit | taṉvayiṟ kiḷappiṟ pulavip poruṭṭē ||
Cf. TP41n.22–24: parattaiyi ṉakaṟciyiṟ parintōṭ kuṟuki | yirattalun teḷittalu meṉaviru vakaiyō | ṭuraittiṟ nāṭṭaṅ kiḻavōṉ mēṉa ||
Cf. IA40: kātaṟ parattai yellārkku murittē ||
Cf. IA43: parattaiyiṟ pirinta kiḻavōṉ maṉaivi | pūppiṉ puṟappā ṭīraṟu nāḷu | nīttakaṉ ṟuṟaita laṟattā ṟaṉṟē ||
Cf. IAC43, p. 235: aḵtāmāṟu: talaimakaṉ parattaiyiṟpirinta kālattut talaimakaṭkup pūpput tōṉṟiṟṟu. tōṉṟat talaimakaṉ uṇarum. eṅṅaṉam uṇarumōveṉiṉ vayilkaḷ uṇarttavē uṇarumeṉpatu.

Based on the size of the lost portion of C1, Cām is a reasonable conjecture. It also, at least, mirrors a koḷu that one finds in later kōvai-s. Cf. Kalaicaikkōvai 410, composed in the eighteenth century, which UVC published in 1935. This may have been his inspiration for the conjecture, apart from what makes sense in this poetic context.

It is not clear what exactly happened in C2. x varai nātaṉ (‘the man from the land with the x mountains’) is a common epithet for the hero in Caṅkam and post-Caṅkam literature, but C1 very clearly reads akal vayal ūraṉ (‘the man from the village with the vast paddy-fields’), which makes good sense and is attested in the Kīḻkkaṇakku corpus, in Aintiṇai Aimpatu 23.1.

One has to assume the C1 reading is either the result of a misapplied sandhi, using the wrong intervocalic glide, or scribal error where the strong verbal root vicai-ttal (‘to hasten’) was conjugated with the wrong suffix, or a k was missed out. The correct form should be vicaikkuvaṉ. If that was the intended reading, it is not clear what it would mean. UVC’s emendation makes good sense and is minimal. Although incorrect glides are not generally a feature of C1, icaikuvaṉ (‘I will speak’) is the most plausible reading.

Eyes reddening is a common trope in Tamil poetry, and considering the surrounding poems, all of which concern the anger of the heroine, cē-ttal is the more likely reading. cōrntaṉaḷ would also make sense though. In that case, the eyes of the heroine would become dejected, as opposed to red (through either crying, anger, or both).

There is no reason why one would expect gemination here, and the only quasi-parallel I have found in the corpus of the C1 reading is sometimes transmitted with gemination and sometimes without (Tirumuṟai 11.030.8), and is found there in a context that would not make sense in this poem. UVC’s two proposed emendations, the first in C2 and the second in Cām, are hard to disambiguate. As I understand it, they both mean much the same – ‘from today’ (for a short discussion on other possibilities, see the note to the translation). ūḻiṉ has to be understood as a contracted form of ūḻiyiṉ. It is attested in PN 237.10 and NA 367.6, and reported as a variant to KT 270.2 by Wilden. It is printed by UVC in his 1937 edition of the KT. I consider this the lectio difficilior when judged against C2.
